How close does each run come to the road?

Closest approach of each run's flow (peak thickness > 0.1 m) to where the avalanche path crosses the road; each run is counted once. The first bar holds runs whose flow touches the road anywhere. Bars are grouped by friction setting.

Methodology

Terrain

Elevation: 260910_LoneTree_Full_Path_Bare_Ground-DSM.tiff (EPSG:26913, 5.50 cm cells), block-averaged to a 1 m grid (1649 x 879 cells at 1 m). Outside the surveyed area the grid is nodata, so the surveyed area is the simulation domain: flow that leaves it is removed. AvaFrame then remeshes the DEM to a 5 m computational mesh, so detail finer than that is averaged before the solver runs. The hillshade in the maps is from the 1 m grid.

Vegetation in the surface. Although the file is labelled bare ground, individual tree and shrub crowns are visible in it: relative to a 15 m median-filtered surface, the start zone has bumps of +5.7 m (95th percentile) to +10 m (99th), the forest beside the path up to about +14 m, and the open path gully about +2 m. They were removed before the runs (next paragraph).

Vegetation removed. Tree and shrub crowns were filtered out of the 1 m grid before the runs (siteTools/groundFilter.py): grey-scale openings with windows of 3, 5, 9, 15, 21 m flag a cell as vegetation when it stands more than 0.5 m + 0.15 × window above the opened surface (the window term keeps convex ground such as ridges and gully banks); flagged cells are filled by interpolation from the surrounding ground. 29% of the cells were flagged; the height removed there has a median of 4.69 m and a 95th percentile of 16.85 m (maximum 31.1 m). Low shrubs (about 1–2 m) are partly left in the surface. The filter is a simple morphological one, not a lidar ground classification; the open gully floor, which has little vegetation, changed by a few centimetres.

Release area

The release area is the polygon Lone_Tree_Bowl_SZ.kml (2.28 ha planimetric), used as drawn. Release thickness is uniform over the zone and is the varied parameter.

Simulations

Dense-flow avalanche simulations with AvaFrame com1DFA (version 2.2b1.post1.dev2+g40a15f536). Constant for all runs: snow density 300 kg/m³, 5 m computational mesh, release area as above, all other parameters at AvaFrame defaults except the shrub settings below. The only input that differs between rows is the release thickness (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2 m); each value is a separate simulation. The size column is the destructive size implied by the release mass alone, using the typical masses of the scale (D1 10 t, D2 100 t, D3 1,000 t, D4 10,000 t), rounded to the nearest half size. Real size classes also depend on destructive potential, so this is a rough guide. The D2 row releases a smaller polygon, McClure_D2_assumed.geojson, with 0.5 m thickness: an assumed D2-sized slab (about 100 t): a 12.9 m-radius patch at the top of the start zone (2,894 m, about 38°). Its location is an assumption, not an observed D2 outline. Recorded D2 and D1.5 avalanches on this path have not reached the road; the one known run past the road was on 24 February 2010. Friction is set per run by AvaFrame from the release volume (next section).

Shrubs (resistance area)

Shrubs about 1–1.5 m high cover the whole path. In this series they are a com1DFA resistance area covering the whole surveyed domain except the road and the release polygon. Where flow in that area is faster than 6 m/s and deeper than 0.6 m, an extra velocity-squared drag is applied (cResH = 0.01 1/m); where it is slower or shallower, snow is taken out of the flow (detrainment, detK = 5). Flow deeper than the shrub height (1.5 m, forestThMax) or faster than 40 m/s is taken to override the shrubs, which then stop acting in that cell for the rest of the run. Apart from forestThMax, these are AvaFrame's default values, which were set up for forest, not shrubs, and are marked in AvaFrame as still needing calibration. The shrubs are treated as standing above the snow; a snowpack that buries them would remove most of their effect. Compare with the series without shrubs.

The release polygon is left out because snow starting from rest is slower than the detrainment threshold: with shrubs there, com1DFA takes thin releases out of the flow before they move. That would express shrubs anchoring the slab, which is a question of whether it releases at all, not of how far it runs; the release thickness scenarios assume it has released.

Friction model: how and why each depth got its class

How. Friction was set with samosATAuto. AvaFrame computes each simulation's release volume and picks one of three calibrations of the samosAT friction model by volume: samosATSmall (μ = 0.22) below 25,000 m³, samosATMedium (μ = 0.17) from 25,000 to 60,000 m³, and standard samosAT (μ = 0.155) above 60,000 m³. The class is chosen per depth, not by hand; the table shows what each depth got (release volume = initial simulated mass / density).

Why. The calibrations assume that larger avalanches are less resisted (lower μ). Release thickness changes the volume from 320 to 61,262 m³, so one fixed class would be mis-calibrated for some of the depths. In particular samosATSmall is meant for volumes below 25,000 m³; only the D2, 0.25 m, 0.5 m, 0.75 m scenarios are below that and use it. An earlier version of this analysis used samosATSmall for all depths, including ones far above that volume, and was replaced for that reason.

Caveat. The class boundaries are step changes. Where a depth sits just on one side of a boundary, the friction jumps between neighbouring depths, so part of the difference between those rows is a friction change, not only a thickness change. Closest to a boundary: 0.75 m (22,870 m³ vs the 25,000 m³ limit), 2 m (61,262 m³ vs the 60,000 m³ limit).

Sensitivity check. A separate test (roadReach.py, thicknesses 0.25–2 m) ran every depth with both samosATMedium and samosAT. Whether the flow reached or crossed the road was the same under both classes at every depth tested; the peak pressure on the road differed by up to a factor of 1.08. The test did not include every depth shown above.

Outputs shown

Peak flow thickness (m), velocity (m/s) and pressure (kPa): the maximum reached at each cell during the simulation, not a snapshot. Cells are shown where peak thickness exceeds 0.1 m. Colour scales are shared across panels. The readout gives each run's values at the cursor, its easting/northing (EPSG:26913), and how many runs reach that cell.

Road reference. "Reaches" and "crosses" mean the flow touches the hill-side and far-side road edge lines (same test as roadReach.py). Distances in the maps and the histogram are measured to one point: where the avalanche path meets the hill-side edge. The path is traced by steepest descent (D8, on the pit-filled 5 m DEM) from the highest cell reached by at least half of the runs. The trace stops 40 m from the road, because closer in it would turn along the road-cut ditch, and its direction over the last 100 m is projected onto the road. The "m short of the road edge" in the panel titles is instead the gap to the nearest point of the edge line, so the two distances differ.

Limitations

  • Results are from a single deterministic model setup and have not been calibrated or validated against observed events at this site.
  • Friction classes come from volume bands and change in steps; a class change between depths is a modelling choice, not a measured difference.
  • Release thickness is a scenario input, not a measurement; it is uniform over the whole release polygon.
  • Shrubs (about 1-1.5 m) cover the start zone and the path. The plain series does not model them; the shrub series adds them as an uncalibrated resistance area outside the release polygon. Neither models shrubs anchoring the slab in the start zone.
  • Peak flow thickness where the gully reaches the road is 3-5 m even for the thinnest release. It is the maximum during the run, not a deposit depth, and has not yet been checked in detail.
